details.sortie: "I will walk with you in love."—Phil. 9.

When Onésimius returns, what opportunity will Philoimus have? According to the situation, Philoimus has great authority to discipline him. But how would he discipline him? What would the slaves say in the assembly? Would there be divisions among the masters and slaves on this issue? Even if such things happen, can Philoimus still praise the peace in the assembly before sending Onésimius back? (Eph. 6:21, 22; Col. 4:7-9) By examining these answers, we can understand what Philoimus, Onesimus, and Philippi would say when Onésimus returns.

Paul exhorted Philemon. (Philem. 4, 5,7) Whenever anyone oppresses us, a great strength arises within us. Why is that? Because there is a feeling of being less than others in many people. We often think and discuss about things like, "Do I need to see or not, do I need to serve others or not, does my service have any value?" It is natural, but due to this, we get discouraged, struggle with small issues, and feel that we are not good enough or better than others. This leads to unrest among us. When someone oppresses us with such feelings, the oppression intensifies even more. (Col. 12:25) We become patient when we love those who love us and value us. Don't we also want to give this patience to our brothers-sisters? Definitely! So, look for opportunities to forgive those who oppress you. You don't get a fruitful result from every effort you make in relationships, but you should forgive every effort made by others. In short, forgive those who oppress you after seeing their miserable condition.

We will speak against those who oppress others and do evil deeds. But how can we break the peace between us from the beginning? He tried to reconcile with his brother Philemon, to cut off the relationship that caused trouble. Personally, it is not worth it at all. According to Roman law, a slave has the right to run away to his master's place. So, he ran for about 1,400 kilometers, spent money, and endured hardship to reach his master's place. If he ran away, he would be free and could continue his education. This is not a matter of shame! Is it not worth going to see Philemon again? If so, he should not think about running away. He decided to cut off the peace with his brother Philemon.

Philemon loved his fellow believers. (Philem. 5) Philemon's name means "lover" or "one who loves." He lived up to his name, loving others and showing love within. This trait also helped him forgive Onesimus when he returned. In his letter to the Colossians, Paul said that love "fills up what is lacking in Christ’s afflictions for the body of Christ" (Col. 3:14). In essence, no characteristic can help as much as love in achieving peace and unity. How much we love others, including forgiving them and being kind to them, is the ultimate measure of this. (1 Cor. 13:4-7) Now we understand how Philemon embodied this in his own life.

Why would God allow us to have "one another in every matter"? When our brothers and sisters trouble us or hurt us, the Bible teaches that we should forgive them. In the same breath, the Bible also speaks about Jehovah’s lofty ideal. We know that God considers us incomplete, so He expects more from us than what we can do on our own. He sees the best in us rather than our weaknesses. Therefore, He shows us great tolerance and mercy. (Psalm 103:13, 14; 130:3) So when we try to see our brothers and sisters as Jehovah does, we often end up disappointed because they can be irritating. They can also show irritation in matters concerning us. For example, if you try to estimate how much a pile of stones weighs by looking at it, you will be disappointed if there are no stones to see. Similarly, if you try to see the best in your brothers and sisters, you may find them irritating and unable to forgive.

Doors at city gates are where ammaku happens. One can say that the names given to some doors there are for ammaka. For example, the Door of Chephus, the Door of Gedor, and so on.—Jdg. 1:10; Jos. 5:2.

Men of valor encouraged the Israelites to go out and fight against the inhabitants near the city gates. Since the people living there were told that others knew about it, they could only say what was necessary. (1 Kings 22:10; Jeremiah 17:19, 20) For example, Ahab told Yahweh to speak through him to the Israelites regarding this matter. (2 Kings 10:8-10) Also, King Hezekiah encouraged his army commanders to rely on the Lord at the city gates. —2 Chronicles 32:6-8

Since we resolved to love Jehovah from the moment we decided to hate Satan, if we are near Jehovah, Satan knows that he will have to destroy us. Therefore, we made it our goal to keep away from Jehovah. We are trying to plant doubts such as “Is Jehovah really concerned about our welfare?”—2 Corinthians 11:14; James 1:6.

After about five decades on earth, Satan tempted Jesus to worship him instead of God after he came down from heaven. Thus, spreading narrow-minded and hateful doctrines, he used others to persecute Jesus with false charges until finally, he had Jesus crucified.—Matt 11:19; 27:27-31; Mark 14:55, 56; John 8:41-45.

When using Satan's main tool in our times—whether regarding Jehovah or Jesus, without knowing them personally—to lie and deceive, he says, "The kidnapper comes that you may be kidnapped." (Joh 8:44) For example, Jehovah and Jesus themselves lied to the crowds without knowing them personally, trying to trap them in their lies. (2 Cor 4:3, 4) The judge of the young man was one and the same as the kidnapper, fully playing the role of the kidnapper. People kissed him completely with their lips. Such worship is not pleasing to Jehovah or Jesus. (Matt 4:10; Joh 4:23) These kidnappers, having failed to capture the kidnappers, find it difficult to manifest themselves; they can also offer us opposition from the kidnappers.

If we were to say that Satan speaks the truth about 12 canines, we would distance ourselves from Jehovah. Sharann B says: "When students, my loved ones, speak to me about my thoughts on dogs in school, they fade away. I retreat into the social media world where I can think about what these people say. Reluctantly, I distance myself from Jehovah, my family, and my brothers-sisters in the congregation." What did she do when it came to the matter of dogs, she pushed Satan away and turned towards Jehovah. How could we help her do that?

We greatly value and study the Bible so that its contents about Jehovah, Jesus Christ become precious to us. (Psalm 119:19) Toward Jehovah and Jesus Christ, as humans, we find what is pleasing when we meditate on them with all our heart, regarding them as our delight. The Bible shows us that Jehovah and Jesus love us. For example, just as a mother cherishes her child, so Jehovah cherishes his people more than a mother cherishes her child. (Isaiah 49:15) Similarly, he regards those who cherish his name as valuable possessions. (Malachi 3:16, 17, context) Jesus also says that he gave his life for us. When we consider what Jesus said about this, it means how much he loves us.—John 15:12, 13.
Regarding Jehovah and Jesus, what recent restrictions did Satan impose?

We declare that the sufferings which come to us are not from Satan in any way. For even if our sufferings are due to the 'world's pressure,' they are for us. Therefore, people will think about and promote them accordingly. From this, the Lord's people will also experience hardships and necessities. —1 Cor. 2:12; 1 Yong. 5:19.
I now see that I am the creator, that He has chosen me, and that He understands my lot. Because of this change in my mind, it alters my life how He wills.

I went to visit a small village in the French countryside that has been working hard. In nature's embrace, it grows hemp, produces opium, and heavily indulges in smoking, yet finds meaning in life. However, for the young people, the story is different; they work for five days and party for two days.

If many people gather together, it's called a crowd. None of us in our group are pushy people, but we are a community where each one respects others despite our different cultures and backgrounds. However, there are also problems and losses in our group, and I realized that we often discuss our needs and issues related to small businesses. Problems in society have also become more prominent among us. Sometimes a few people come and go for days or even months, and now I am here for about two years.

I realized that God was considering creating me when I overheard Him saying He wanted to know more about humans. A friend from our group invited me to meet Jehovah's witnesses. They gave us a book titled "You Can Live Forever on Earth" and I read it too. It really excited me! The idea of transforming into a being that can live forever on Earth, instead of just existing temporarily, really excited me. With this new earth, we could live peacefully without dying, and enjoy life. This would never happen to me! If our Creator has such an amazing future planned for us, then He must have a great purpose in mind, and He still has time to change His mind.

I decided to drop the subjects I was studying. Before going back to poppy cultivation, I decided to try quitting opium. I won't go back to it if I fail. I also decided to attend meetings. In one meeting, when my sister told me she would help me quit smoking, she said she would do it in the palace itself.

We have a zealous sister named Cladeen in our congregation, who got infected. She enthusiastically participates in meetings, and her love for Jehovah has grown even in her comments. I want to learn more about her. Before all that, I didn't know whether she liked being a real missionary or not. After she said she liked it, we sent her off in April 2000.

From my experience, I have a job called hyperhydrosis. Due to this, my hands sweat a lot; if I am nervous, even more. When I am in tension, that is, when I am present in a gathering and get nervous, it gets worse. However, when I pray for peace of mind, it calms down. Still, without relying on Jehovah, tension increases and so does sweating.

I first attended the assembly where I tasted the bridegroom in my life. Jehovah, our Creator, caresses His worshippers greatly. Also, as a brother who leads in organizations and government, he told me to rebuke them kindly. Jehovah touched me with his embrace through loved ones in the world. But Jehovah gave me many more beloveds than that. A wife like Claudia was also one of them. In the future, I look forward to living forever for Jehovah for many more years.—Mark 10:29, 30
(In 2006, there was a performance at the Chinese language meeting.)

As servants of Jehovah, we are not to engage in the wars that are taking place on this earth. (Isaiah 2:4; Hosea 18:36) However, the Bible does speak of a war that we are to wage, a battle using the spiritual army of those faithful and upright. (See Ephesians 6:11, 12.) And can we possibly win without powerful weapons? Not at all! With Jehovah’s help, it is possible. But we must rely on him. Otherwise, we will have to face Satan and his demons, as well as brothers and sisters who may be deceived.

Let the sun be eclipsed in Rajain's matter. He hates the claim that is so precious to him. David was a valiant warrior, and seeing this strength, Saul initially loved him greatly. (1 Sam. 18:5) But as time passed, seeing more renowned figures than himself, Saul became envious and bitter towards David. (1 Sam. 18:9-11) When Saul tried to crush David, he turned to Satan. For, when David was anointed king over Israel by Yahweh, Saul tried to thwart Yahweh’s will. Seeing Saul’s attempt to eclipse Yahweh’s anointed, Satan rejoiced. If it were not for Yahweh’s command, he would have found joy in destroying Saul.

When sisters or brothers complain to us about each other, let us focus on one thing: they too are imperfect and make mistakes. Indeed, when we work together with them, we often find fault in their dealings. (Prov. 7:20) Then, the Bible advises that one should show forbearance when another can offer comfort in one area. When anyone wrongs us, we should forgive immediately. (Col. 3:12-14) We should love our sisters and brothers, and be like one family, as Jehovah, Jesus Christ’s creation, desires. —Joh. 17:20, 21.

After many years of wandering, Jesus came to earth as Messiah and experienced numerous sufferings. For example, those who betrayed him were his close friends. (Mark 3:21) His claims about God were often met with skeptical challenges. (Luke 11:15, 16) The disciples who had been with Jesus for such a long time could not believe he was going to be betrayed. (Matt. 26:14-16) The chief priests plotted with the authorities to arrest him. (Mark 15:1, 13-15) Yet, despite the great betrayal, Jesus only served Yahweh and never sought to escape; he did not even turn to his disciples for help. When he was arrested, a servant girl at the gate accused him, but Jesus denied it, and the servant girl was struck mute. (Luke 22:50, 51) In all these situations, instead of considering how to escape from those who wronged him, Jesus focused on doing the work given to him by Yahweh.

15 Yahweh sees every oppression that befalls us. He knows even when we groan under it. (Psalm 37:18) It is not within our power to solve the problems of this world. (Proverbs 1:15) But it is within His power. The wrongs done to us by Satan and his demons will be righted by His kingdom. (1 John 3:8; Psalm 21:5) With patience, we will wait for Him, loving His people. We will also use our time and strength to help make more people loved by Yahweh.

How will Philippians react when Onesimus returns? Legally, he has the right to severely punish that slave. Will he use that right? How will the church respond? What if other masters and slaves in the church become divided by the issue between Philippians and Onesimus? Paul knew that their problem could cause the church to lose harmony. Therefore, he wrote a letter to Philippians and entrusted it to Timothy to deliver (Eph 6:21, 22; Col 4:7-9). At the same time, Paul also sent a letter to the church in Colosse. Based on these two letters, what can we learn from Paul, Onesimus, and Philippians?

Paul commends Philemon (Philemon 4, 5, 7). All of us need praise. Why? One reason is that many of us struggle with feelings of insecurity. For example, we worry about our appearance, wonder if others value us, or fear losing a precious gift. These emotions are normal. However, sometimes they can cause us to be overly anxious or hypersensitive, defensive, or even competitive. Such feelings can hinder our efforts to promote harmony. Someone can handle feelings of insecurity better if they receive praise (Cham 12:25). Praise helps them feel loved and valued. Do you want to help others feel that way? If so, look for opportunities to sincerely praise others. Don’t just praise their good results but also their efforts. In short, if you see something good in someone, praise it.

10 All of us say or do things that hurt others at some point. Onesimus’s mirror teaches us how to mend relationships when that happens. He did something that seemed simple but is often not easy. Onesimus took responsibility and made his part to reconcile with Philemon. Undoubtedly, Onesimus knew that Roman law required him to return to his master. So, he undertook a difficult and costly journey over more than 1,400 km to return to Philemon. Onesimus had to be ready to give up his freedom and possibly accept other consequences of his actions. This must not have been an easy decision. And what if he felt justified in running away from Philemon? Even if he felt that way, he did not let it stop him from returning and doing what he could to promote reconciliation with Philemon, now his fellow believer.

13 Philippians loved fellow believers (Phil 5). His name means “love,” and he lived up to his name. Philippians was known for his prominent love, a quality that helped him forgive Onesimus. In his letter to the Philippian church in Colosse, Paul described love as “the bond of perfect unity.” In other words, love is the most important quality that contributes to unity and harmony. The more we love others, the easier it is to forgive and treat them kindly (1 Cor 13:4-7). Let's see what helped Philippians strengthen his love.

What is Paul’s intention when he advises us to "bear with one another"? It is that we need to be patient and kind to fellow believers, even when they irritate or hurt us. In the same sentence, Paul emphasizes the example of Jehovah’s love and forgiveness. He has reasonable expectations of his servants. He knows our limitations but focuses on the good qualities in us (Ps 103:13, 14; 130:3). Therefore, he continues to show boundless mercy and compassion toward us (Ps 119:22, 23). If we try to see our brothers as Jehovah sees them, we will find it easier to endure their mistakes, just as they should endure ours. To illustrate: If we remember how beautiful a tree will look when it blossoms, we have motivation to care for it even when it is not in bloom. Similarly, if we remember the good points of our brothers, we will have motivation to forgive and treat them kindly, even when they disappoint us.

Merchants sold goods near the city gates. Some of the gates in Jerusalem, such as the Gate of Sheep and the Fish Gate, may have been named after the goods sold nearby.—Neh 3:1; John 5:2.

Faithful men encouraged the people of Israel who were at the city gates to trust in Jehovah. The prophets and others spoke to the people at the gates because they knew that the people often gathered there (1 Kings 22:10; Jer 17:19, 20). For example, Jehu declared before the people that Jehovah had fulfilled his word against the house of Ahab (2 Kings 10:8-10). King Hezekiah gathered the army commanders at the city gates to encourage them to rely on Jehovah's help.—2 Chron 32:6-8.

Since we decided to serve Jehovah, Satan and the demons have become constant attackers against us. But Satan knows that he cannot defeat us when we have the support of Jehovah. So, the Devil strives to make us turn our backs on him so that we lose that support. One way he does this is by trying to make us think that Jehovah and his Son do not really care about us.—2 Cor 11:14; 1 John 1:6.

Five centuries after Jesus lived on earth, Satan tried to prevent people from following him. One way he did this was by using religious leaders filled with hatred and others to spread lies about Jesus. Eventually, they caused him to be executed as a criminal.—Read Matthew 11:19; 27:27-31; Mark 14:55, 56; John 8:41-45.

Today, one of Satan's main schemes is to obscure the truth about Jehovah and Jesus. As the "father of lies," he spreads falsehoods about them through false religions (John 8:44). For example, he causes people to be mentally blind and unaware of the true identities of Jehovah and his Son (2 Corinthians 4:3, 4). The Christian religion often teaches that the Father and the Son are equal. The result is that people ignore the Father, whom they do not know, and worship the Son. But neither Jehovah nor Jesus accepts such worship (Matthew 4:10; John 4:23). When people are spiritually blind in this way, it can be very difficult for us to reason with them. They may even oppose our preaching work.

Listening to Satan's propaganda can cause us to drift away from Jehovah. A young woman named Shannon shared, "It took me some time to realize that the moral standards taught at school and those I associated with had distorted my views of right and wrong. The more time I spent on social media, the more I wanted to emulate the people I met there. As a result, I gradually drifted away from Jehovah, my family, and fellow believers." Later on, Shannon returned to her Heavenly Father and escaped Satan's trap. What helped her do this?

By studying the Bible carefully, we become more confident that Jehovah and Jesus are on our side (Ps 22:19). This book tells about men and women who trusted in Jehovah and Jesus. When we reflect on how those two cared for them, we will trust Jehovah and Jesus even more. The Bible also contains many assurances that these two love us. For example, Jehovah describes his love for his people as being stronger than a mother’s love for her child (Isa 49:15). Jehovah regards those who honor his name as his “precious inheritance” (Mal 3:16, 17). The Bible also shows how deeply Jesus loved us by recording what he said about his sacrifice.—John 15:12, 13.
How did Satan lie about Jehovah and Jesus in the past?

Satan does not directly cause all the problems we encounter. But he stands behind "the spirit of this world," which influences those who oppose God's people, causing them to mistreat God’s children. Therefore, whether directly or indirectly, Satan is responsible for many of the difficulties and trials we face in the spiritual battle.—1 Cor 2:12; 1 John 5:19.
However, now I am certain that God not only exists but also cares about me regardless of my flaws. Let me tell you what changed my thinking and how this faith has transformed my life.

I returned to one of the remote villages in French Guiana, where I once served in the military. I thought I would be happier living closer to nature, smoking marijuana, and enjoying life. But after some time, the old life repeated itself. I worked all week just to party on weekends.

We want to rebuild the world in the way we are living it. No one in the community has more rights than others, and everyone respects each other regardless of their background. However, I realize that ultimately, each person still seeks their own interests and all have weaknesses. And the issues that society outside must face will eventually appear within our circle as well. Some people stay in the community for just a few days, while others stay for weeks or months. And I stayed for over two years.

When reflecting on the beginning of my prayers, I felt that God had noticed me and seen that I wanted to know more about Him. A friend in the community met Jehovah's Witnesses and received the book You Can Live Forever in a Perfect World on Earth. When I read that book, I was amazed at what I learned! I really like the prospect of living forever on a transformed earth in paradise. That is exactly what I was looking for. I always wished to live under ideal conditions on earth, in peace with those I love, and never to die. I wanted to draw closer to the generous God who has the intention of giving us such a wonderful future.

I learned many things from the Bible and understood what changes I needed to make. I decided to quit smoking and using marijuana. Right after making that decision, I threw the remaining cigarettes and marijuana into the fire and never smoked again. I started attending some group meetings. At one of the meetings, I asked a man to cut my long hair, and he did it right in Heaven's Water Room.

In the church, a beautiful sister named Claudine caught my attention. I noticed she was very enthusiastic about her ministry, and her comments during group meetings showed that she loved Jehovah very much. I wanted to get to know Claudine, but first I wanted to know if she aspired to be a minister. It was great that she did! We got married in April 2000.

I also face another difficulty. Since childhood, I have suffered from hyperhidrosis, meaning my body sweats excessively. This condition particularly affects my hands and worsens in stressful situations, such as when I present a lecture to many people at a conference or assembly. But I can mitigate this reaction by pleading with Jehovah to grant me mental peace. The problem still exists, but as I rely more on him, I remain calmer and sweat less.

When attending my first convention, I learned that the Almighty Creator God always cares for those who worship him. Thanks to this, I have received many blessings. He has helped me develop the right perspective on authority and taught me humility. I stopped associating with worldly friends so that I could live according to God's standards, but he compensated for that by giving me many true friends. I have found an amazing wife. I also have the wonderful hope of enjoying God's generosity forever.—Mark 10:29, 30.

As servants of Jehovah, we do not participate in human conflicts (Isaiah 2:4; John 18:36). However, the Bible mentions a battle that none of us can avoid—the battle against the wicked spirits. (Read Ephesians 6:11, 12). How can we triumph over such powerful enemies? The most important thing is to rely on Jehovah’s support. But we also need to recognize the schemes that Satan and his demons use to attack us and our fellow believers.

Let's look at a case. King Saul began to hate the loyal David. At first, Saul loved this young man. He was very impressed by David's fighting ability (1 Sa 18:5). But over time, Saul became extremely jealous when he saw that the people loved David more than him. So, he tried many times to kill David (1 Sa 18:9-11). If David were killed, that would be exactly what Satan wanted. Why? Under the guidance of the Lord, David had been anointed as the next king of Israel (1 Sa 16:13). Satan would be very pleased if that plan failed. Imagine how delighted he must have been to see Saul's jealousy and his efforts to harm the one whom the Lord chose as the next king.

When a fellow believer says or does something that hurts you, remember that you too have sinned like him or her at times. If we spend much time working with our fellow believers, we will tend to see their faults (Ecclesiastes 7:20). In such cases, follow the Bible’s advice to bear with one another. And if someone has hurt you, quickly forgive them (Colossians 3:12-14). By preserving the unity of the spiritual family, we please Jehovah and Jesus.—John 17:20, 21.

Many centuries later, after Jesus, whom God promised would come as the Messiah, faced numerous trials and challenges on Earth, he encountered difficulties. For instance, some of Jesus' family members thought he had lost his mind (Mark 3:21). Religious leaders often questioned his authority to teach the people about God, even suggesting that his power came from demons (Luke 11:15, 16). One of Jesus' apostles betrayed him (Matthew 26:14-16). The high priests conspired with the rulers to condemn Jesus to death (Mark 15:1, 13-15). But Jesus did not let opposition slow him down in serving Jehovah. Jesus never sought revenge. When he was arrested, the apostle Peter tried to defend him, cutting off the ear of the high priest's servant. But Jesus was not pleased with Peter's violent reaction and healed the servant by miracle (Luke 22:50, 51). In all these cases, Jesus did not allow challenges to distract him or seek revenge.

We will waste time and effort trying to right every wrong we see or endure today (Ecclesiastes 1:15). The Lord knows what we are going through (Psalm 37:18). Soon, Heaven will remedy all the harm that Satan and his agents have caused (1 John 3:8; Revelation 21:5). Until then, we need to continue being patient and showing love to everyone. We should focus our time and energy on helping as many people as possible become friends of the Lord.

What does Paul instruct Philemon to do regarding slave Onesimus? Legally, Onesimus had the right to be freed. But did he do that? Was this an act of rebellion? No, this action led to reconciliation between the Lord and His people? Paul knew that this situation could be resolved with peace. Therefore, he wrote to Philemon from prison in Colossians, asking him to receive Onesimus as both a brother and a slave. (Col. 4:7-9; see also the testimony about Tychicus in Colossians 4:7, nwtsty.) At the same time, Paul also wrote to Tychicus for Onesimus. In this article, we will delve into what Paul, Onesimus, and Philemon learned from Paul’s letters to Colossians and Philemon.

Paul wrote to Philemon. (Phlm. 4, 5, 7) We all need to be reconciled. Why? One reason is that many of us have been wronged and feel the need to reconcile. We may not have peace in our hearts if others do not love us or if we fail to forgive their offenses. These feelings are common. Yet, such matters can cause unrest, leading to restlessness, anxiety about the state of our relationships, or even to a spirit of contention—qualities that can hinder our efforts to promote peace. It is much better for a person to be reconciled and at peace, especially when they are trying to foster harmony. (Mt. 12:25) Reconciliation confirms that we are loved and forgiven. So, do we love and help others in this way? If so, seek opportunities to reconcile from within your own home. Others may already be reconciled due to their good work, but also because of their own struggles. Sometimes, you will find someone who needs reconciliation, and you should reconcile.

10 She saw that some things needed to be addressed and settled. For example, Onesimus taught how to forgive those who wronged you. Although his task was simple, it often required great courage. With his trust and encouragement, Onesimus managed to travel over 1,400 miles to reconcile with Philemon. He needed to be ready to fight for his freedom and even risk other relationships that did not align with his principles. This mission was not easy. And what if he had believed he had the right to force Philemon to forgive him? If he had thought this way, he would not have been able to reconcile with Philemon while still being free to work towards peace between them as brothers.

Filemon loved his brother. (Phlm. 5) Filemon was known as "The Lover" because of the deep love he had, a quality that was crucial for reuniting Onesimus. Moreover, in his letter to the Colossians, where he mentions Filemon, Paul affirms that love is "the bond of perfect unity." (Col. 3:14.) In another passage, there is no other quality that more significantly contributes to peace and unity than love. Even if one loves others more, they still remain a little less to us in our efforts to reconcile and forgive. (1 Cor. 13:4-7) Thus, love helped Filemon to reconcile.

17 Paul asks what “fullness” means when he says “I will be filled.” He was starving and fainting from hunger and thirst even as they were being filled. In the psalm, Paul sets an example of Jehovah who feeds his people. Jehovah is full of compassion and mercy toward those who do his work. We see our weakness but we have a good thought. That is why he wants to show the fullness that comes with his mercy. (Ps. 103:13, 14; 130:3) Because of this, if you do everything to please Jehovah as he sees fit, you will be more inclined to show compassion and to be filled with mercy—just as you are filled with compassion when you show mercy. For example: If you learn how to forgive someone who has wronged you, you will be able to forgive them freely. 3 What would Philemon have done upon Anencissus’s return? Legally, he had every right to punish him harshly. Would he exercise this right? How would the community react? And what if there had been a split among the masters and other slaves due to this matter? Paul knew that this situation could disrupt the peace of the community. At the same time, he also sent a letter to the community in Colosse. Let us reflect on lessons we can learn from Paul, Anencissus, and Philemon as found in these two letters.

6 Paul commended Philemon. (Philem 4, 5, 7) Everyone needs commendation. Why? One reason is that many lack self-confidence and security. Perhaps we worry about our outward appearance, or others’ perceptions of us, or fear losing a cherished service opportunity. These feelings are natural. Yet, they may make us overly anxious or sensitive. They also push us to take a defensive stance or even nurture a competitive spirit; these traits might hinder our efforts to promote peace. But when an individual receives commendation, they can better overcome feelings of self-doubt. (Acts 12:25) Commendation affirms that they are loved and valued by others. Would you like this to be your impact on others? Then seek opportunities to genuinely commend them. Don’t commend them only for good results, but also for the work they do. Simply, when you see something beautiful, say something beautiful.

We all say and do things that annoy others. And Ansimus teaches us how to respond with peace when this happens. He did something simple, but often difficult: he admitted his mistake and took on his role to reconcile with Philemon. Of course, Ansimus knew that Roman law required him to return to his master. For that, he undertook a costly and exhausting journey of more than 1,400 kilometers to return to Philemon. He had to be prepared to give up his freedom, and perhaps accept other consequences for his actions. This decision could not have been easy. What if Ansimus felt justified in running away from Philemon? If that was his feeling, he did not let it stop him from returning to his master and doing everything he could to promote peace between them as spiritual brothers.

13 Philippians loved his brothers. (Phil 5) Phil's name was fitting for him. His name means "lover." He was well-known for his distinctive love, which was the primary quality that would help him forgive Onesimus. In fact, in the letter Paul wrote to the Philippians in Colosse, he described love as "the bond of perfect unity." (Read Colossians 3:14.) In other words, no quality contributes more to peace and unity than love. The more we love others, the easier it becomes for us to forgive them and treat them kindly. (1 Cor 13:4-7) Let's see how this idea applied to Phil's situation.

What did Paul mean when he said, "Bear one another’s burdens”? He encouraged us to be patient with our fellow believers and treat them kindly even when they annoy or hurt us. In the same verse, Paul shed light on the wonderful example of Yahweh. Yahweh has reasonable expectations from his worshippers. He knows well our shortcomings but focuses on our good qualities. (Ps 103:13, 14; 130:3) Thus, he continues to show us his extraordinary kindness and mercy. (Mal 3:22, 23) We too, if we make an effort to see our fellow believers as Yahweh sees them, will find it easier to be patient with them and bear their faults, just as they patiently bear ours and forgive us for our mistakes. For clarification: If we remember the beauty of the plant when it blossoms, we get excited to take care of it even when it has no flowers. Similarly, if we recall the good things about our brothers and sisters, we are motivated to forgive and treat them kindly even when they disappoint us.

(1 Kings 22:10; Jer 17:19, 20) For example, Jahu proclaimed before all the people that Yahweh had fulfilled the words He spoke against the house of Ahab. (2 Kings 10:8-10) And King Hezekiah gathered the military leaders at the city gate to encourage them to rely on Yahweh's assistance. — 2 Chron 32:6-8.

From the moment we decide to serve Yahweh, Satan and his angels become our fierce enemies. But Satan knows that he cannot overcome us as long as Yahweh supports us. Therefore, he wants to undermine this support and tries to lure us away from Yahweh. One way he does this is by sowing doubt in our hearts that Yahweh and His Son are truly on our side. — 2 Cor 11:14; Jas 1:6.

After centuries, when Jesus came to the earth, Satan tried to prevent people from following Jesus. One of the ways he did this was by inciting the bitter religious leaders and others to spread lies about Jesus. In the end, they crucified him as an example of a criminal. — Read Matthew 11:19; 27:27-31; Mark 14:55, 56; John 8:41-45.

Today, one of Satan's primary tactics is to hide the truth about Yahweh and Jesus from people. As the "Father of Lies," he spreads lies about them through false religions. (Jn 8:44) For example, he blinds people so they do not know the true identity of Yahweh and His real Son. (2 Cor 4:3, 4) The Christian world often portrays the Father and the Son as equals. Consequently, people tend to ignore the Father, whom they do not know by name, and worship the Son. But neither Yahweh nor Jesus approve of this worship. (Mt 4:10; Jn 4:23) And when people's minds are blinded in this way, they may not hear us when we try to tell them the truth, and may even resist our work.

If we follow the deception that Satan promotes, we may drift far from Jehovah. A sister named Shanon says: "I needed time to realize that the standards I learned in school and from the people I associate with were confusing my sense of right and wrong. The more time I spent on social media, I wanted to emulate those I met online and adopt their values. Gradually, I began to drift away from Jehovah, from my family, and from my brothers and sisters." But in the end, Shanon found her way back to her Heavenly Father and was saved from Satan's trap. What helped her?

When we contemplate the Holy Scriptures carefully, we strengthen our confidence that Yahweh and Jesus are beside us. (Amos 22:19) For as we read the events that show how much Yahweh and Jesus care for humanity, we are spurred to consider them as friends on whom we can rely. The Holy Scriptures are full of verses that confirm to us that Yahweh and Jesus love us. For example, Yahweh describes his feelings toward his people and says they are stronger than a mother’s feelings toward her infant child. (Isaiah 49:15) Yahweh considers every one who values his name as his “precious possession.” (Malachi 3:16, 17, footnote) We also see the depth of Jesus’ love for us when we read what he said in the Holy Scriptures about the sacrifice he offered. —John 15:12, 13.
How did Satan distort the image of Yahweh and Jesus in the past?

Satan does not directly cause every difficulty we face. But he is responsible for spreading the “spirit of this world” that encourages opponents to treat God’s people badly. Therefore, whether directly or indirectly, Satan is behind many of the challenges we face in our spiritual warfare. — 2 Cor 2:12; 1 John 5:19.
But today, I am not convinced merely that there is a Creator, but that He cares for me despite my weaknesses. Let me tell you what changed my mind and how this reality has turned my life around.

I returned to one of the remote villages in French Guiana where I had served in the army. I hoped that my life would gain a greater meaning if I was surrounded by nature, smoked marijuana, and lived peacefully. But after a short while, my life returned to how it was: I worked every day of the week so I could go to parties at the weekend.

We wanted to change the world to make it like the world we live in. In our gathering, no one had authority over another. We respected each other by looking past our backgrounds. But in the end, I realized that each of us has our weaknesses and strive for our own interests. As time went on, we began facing the same problems that societies face in general. Some stayed in this gathering for just a few days, while others stayed for weeks or months. As for me, I stayed for more than two years.

When I recall the period when I started praying, I feel that the Creator saw my desire to know Him more. One of my friends in the gathering had met Jehovah's Witnesses, and he obtained a book that can enable you to live forever in paradise on earth. And as I read it, I was amazed by what I learned! I loved the hope of living forever on a transformed earth in paradise. This is exactly what I was searching for: to live on earth under ideal conditions in peace with the people I love, without ever tasting the taste of death. So I wanted to draw closer to this gracious Creator who intended to give us this wonderful future.

As I progressed in my studies of the holy book, I made changes in my life. I decided to stop smoking tobacco and marijuana. As soon as I made this decision, I threw what was left of my tobacco and marijuana in the fire, and I never touched cigarettes again after that. I also started attending some gatherings. At one gathering, I asked an older brother to cut my long hair, and he readily complied and cut my hair right there in the hall.

In my community, a beautiful sister named Claudine caught my eye. I noticed that she was enthusiastic in service, and her responses in gatherings showed me that she loves the Lord greatly. I wanted to get to know her better. But first, I wanted to find out if she would like to serve as a missionary. Indeed, this was her desire! We got married in April 2000.

I faced another challenge. Since my childhood, I have suffered from excessive sweating. This problem affects my hands especially. My condition worsens when I am under pressure, for example, when giving a speech in a monthly or annual meeting. But I can alleviate the severity of this situation by praying to Jehovah to give me peace. Of course, the problem hasn't disappeared, but the more I rely on Jehovah, the more I feel calm and sweat less.

At my first annual gathering, I learned that the great Creator, Jehovah, constantly cares for his worshippers. I decided to put him first in my life, and as a result, I received many blessings. He helps me adopt the correct perspective on those in authority and to remain humble. Although I had to stop associating with my worldly friends to live according to Jehovah's standards, he compensated by giving me many true friends. I also found an outstanding wife, and I have the wonderful hope of enjoying Jehovah's generosity forever. —Psalm 10:29, 30.
(To the north) I gave a speech at the Chinese team in 2006

As servants of Jehovah, we do not participate in the wars of this world. (Isaiah 2:4; John 18:36) But the Holy Scriptures speak of a war in which none of us can avoid participating, namely, the war against wicked spirits. (Read Ephesians 6:11, 12.) How can we ensure that we conquer these powerful enemies? First of all, we must rely on Jehovah’s support. But it also requires that we know the tactics that Satan and his demons use against us and our spiritual family.

4 Here is an example of King Saul, who turned against David, the future king. At first, Saul liked this young man very much and was greatly impressed by his fighting abilities. (1 Sam 18:5) But after some time, Saul noticed that David’s popularity was greater than his own, which consumed him with jealousy. As a result, he embarked on a campaign lasting years to kill David. (1 Sam 18:9-11) David’s death would have served Satan’s interests. How so? Under God’s guidance, David had been destined to become Israel’s future king. (1 Sam 16:13) How delighted Satan would be if this purpose failed! Imagine him watching with satisfaction as Saul, the envious one, became obsessed with killing the man whom God chose to be the next king.

When your brother in faith says something that wounds you or does something that irritates you, remember that you too are lacking like him completely. And if you serve closely with one of your brothers, it is logical to expect some friction. (Col 7:20) When that happens, apply the advice given to bear with each other. And if someone hurts you, forgive him quickly. (Col 3:12-14) Work with Jehovah and Jesus to fulfill their purpose that our Christian family remain united. — John 17:20, 21.

After centuries, when the awaited Messiah Jesus came to the earth, he faced numerous challenges. For instance, some members of his family said he had lost his mind. (Mark 3:21) Religious leaders continued to doubt his authority to preach to people. (Luke 11:15, 16) Moreover, one of his closest friends betrayed him. (Matthew 26:14-16) Additionally, the high priests colluded with political authorities to sentence him to death. (Mark 15:1, 13-15) However, Jesus did not allow resistance to weaken his service to Yahweh. He never showed a stance of revenge. When arrested, Peter tried to defend him and cut off the ear of the servant of the high priest. But Jesus did not approve of his violent retaliation and performed a miracle to heal the man. (Luke 22:50, 51) In all these circumstances, Jesus never allowed the challenges he faced to distract or drive him towards revenge.

We will quickly exhaust much of our time and energy if we try to correct all the injustices we see or suffer from each day. (1 Jn 1:15) The Lord knows exactly what we can bear. (Ps 37:18) Soon enough, his kingdom will remove all the harm caused by the devil and his followers. (1 Jn 3:8; Rev 21:5) Until that time, we must remain patient and show love to those near us. We should invest our time and energy in helping as many people as possible become friends of the Lord.
